raw_text:
### Introduction
Cardiac amyloidosis is a progressive, infiltrative cardiomyopathy characterized by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardial tissue [1]. Historically considered a rare, untreatable condition, diagnostic advancements and the introduction of targeted therapeutics have transitioned cardiac amyloidosis into an increasingly recognized and treatable etiology of heart failure [2]. The two primary precursors responsible for cardiac amyloidosis are immunoglobulin light chains (AL) and transthyretin (ATTR) [3]. AL amyloidosis is a clonal plasma cell disorder characterized by the production of unstable monoclonal light chains [3], whereas ATTR amyloidosis arises from the dissociation of the hepatic-synthesized transthyretin tetramer into unstable monomers that misfold and aggregate [4,5]. ATTR occurs in two distinct clinical forms: hereditary (variant, ATTRv), caused by mutations in the *TTR* gene, and wild-type (ATTRwt), an age-related systemic condition that predominantly affects elderly men [6,7].

### Clinical Presentation and Red Flags
Patients with cardiac amyloidosis typically present with symptoms of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [2]. However, key extracardiac clinical clues ("red flags") are vital for early diagnosis. Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, and biceps tendon rupture frequently precede cardiovascular manifestations by several years, particularly in patients with ATTRwt [8]. Autonomic dysfunction, manifesting as orthostatic hypotension or chronic gastrointestinal symptoms, is also common [4]. Electrocardiography (ECG) often shows low QRS voltage, which is highly suggestive when discordant with the severe left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) observed on echocardiography [1].

### Diagnostic Advancements and Algorithms
While traditional diagnosis relied heavily on invasive endomyocardial biopsy [17], contemporary clinical pathways utilize a highly validated non-invasive diagnostic algorithm [15]. Echocardiography serves as the initial screening modality, typically demonstrating symmetric ventricular thickening, a "granular sparkling" myocardial appearance, and a highly specific pattern of apical sparing on longitudinal strain analysis [9,10]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides advanced tissue characterization, revealing diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and substantial elevations in native T1 mapping and extracellular volume (ECV) fraction [11,12].

A critical step in the non-invasive diagnostic pathway is the exclusion of AL amyloidosis, which is a medical emergency. Clinicians must screen for monoclonal proteins using serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis coupled with a serum free light chain (sFLC) assay [13,14]. If clonal free light chains are absent, Technetium-99m pyrophosphate ($^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc}$-PYP), dicarboxydiphosphonate (DPD), or hydroxymethylene diphosphonate (HMDP) scintigraphy is performed [15,16]. Grade 2 or 3 myocardial radiotracer uptake on planar or SPECT imaging, in the absence of a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia, is 99% sensitive and specific for ATTR cardiac amyloidosis, establishing the diagnosis without the need for tissue biopsy [15]. However, if monoclonal proteins are detected, or if scintigraphy yields equivocal results, an endomyocardial biopsy remains mandatory [17]. Biopsy specimens are evaluated using Congo red staining to demonstrate apple-green birefringence under polarized light, followed by mass spectrometry for definitive amyloid typing [18,19].

### Therapeutic Strategies
The management of cardiac amyloidosis differs fundamentally between the AL and ATTR subtypes. In AL amyloidosis, rapid suppression of the toxic clone is paramount to prevent progressive, irreversible organ damage [3,13]. First-line chemotherapy typically involves a combination of cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (CyBorD) [20]. The addition of the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab has dramatically improved hematologic and organ response rates [21]. Eligible patients may also undergo high-dose chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation [22].

For ATTR amyloidosis, current disease-modifying therapies target various steps in the amyloidogenic pathway [2,4]. Transthyretin stabilizers bind to the thyroxine-binding sites on the TTR tetramer, preventing its dissociation into amyloidogenic monomers [4]. Tafamidis, a selective TTR stabilizer, demonstrated a 30% reduction in all-cause mortality and a 32% reduction in cardiovascular hospitalizations in the landmark ATTR-ACT trial, representing the first approved disease-modifying therapy for ATTR cardiomyopathy [23]. Diflunisal, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, also stabilizes TTR but is frequently limited by renal and gastrointestinal toxicities [24].

Alternatively, genetic silencers suppress TTR synthesis in the liver. RNA interference (RNAi) therapeutics, including patisiran [25,26] and vutrisiran [28], as well as the antisense oligonucleotide inotersen [27], have shown notable efficacy in halting neuropathy progression and improving surrogate cardiac markers in clinical trials.

### Supportive Care and Prognosis
Supportive management of heart failure in cardiac amyloidosis requires meticulous volume regulation. Loop diuretics and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are the cornerstones of therapy [29]. Standard heart failure medications—including beta-blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, and calcium channel blockers—are poorly tolerated due to restrictive physiology and fixed stroke volume, and should generally be avoided [30].

### Conclusion
The clinical landscape of cardiac amyloidosis has transitioned from a fatal, underdiagnosed disease to a manageable condition. Modern non-invasive imaging protocols facilitate early detection, while novel stabilizer and silencer therapies offer substantial survival benefits. Increased awareness of clinical "red flags" is essential to ensure early diagnosis and maximize the benefits of emerging disease-modifying therapies.
